problem: "only the MSP430 offers named sleep modes with sub-microsecond wake-up" contradicts the chapter's own table, which lists 8051 Idle/Power-down and PIC18 Sleep as named modes. The wake-up figure is also overstated: waking from LPM3 (DCO off) takes a few microseconds on real parts; only LPM0 wake-up is immediate.
fix: The MSP430 is the only one of the three that grades low power into several named levels, LPM0 to LPM4. The 8051 has two modes (Idle, Power-down) and the PIC18 has one (Sleep). The MSP430 returns from LPM0 within a clock cycle and from LPM3 in a few microseconds, because the DCO must restart.

problem: "The PIC keeps an 8-bit data path and fetches 16-bit instruction words from flash, so it needs banked RAM" gives the wrong cause. Banking comes from the 8-bit address field inside each instruction, not from the 8-bit data path or the flash width. Section 2 states the correct reason, so the lead contradicts it.
fix: The PIC keeps an 8-bit data path and fetches 16-bit instruction words from flash. Because a data address in an instruction is only 8 bits wide, the 1536 bytes of RAM are split into banks reached through the BSR.

problem: "Every instruction is 16 bits wide" is too strong. On the PIC18, GOTO, CALL, MOVFF and LFSR occupy two 16-bit words. The word count 16,384 is still correct because flash is organised as 16-bit words, but a student will be surprised when GOTO eats two words.
fix: Instruction words are 16 bits wide; a few instructions (GOTO, CALL, MOVFF, LFSR) use two words. Flash of 32,768 bytes therefore holds 16,384 instruction words.

problem: pattern[] and i are declared after the TRISB and PORTB statements. Older XC8 projects compile in C90 mode, where all declarations must come before the first statement, so this listing will not build there.
fix: Declare at the top of main: unsigned char pattern[4] = {0x3F, 0x06, 0x5B, 0x4F}; unsigned char i = 0; then TRISB = 0x00; PORTB = 0x00; while (1) { ... }

problem: The constant generator R3 is said to produce "0, 1, 2, −1 or 4". The standard set is 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 and −1; 8 is missing, so the list is incomplete as written.
fix: R3 is a constant generator that produces 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 or −1 without spending an operand field.

problem: "A digitally controlled oscillator (DCO) starts in under a microsecond" is not supported: data sheets quote the DCO wake-up time in the microsecond range (a few microseconds), and the chapter gives no part number.
fix: A digitally controlled oscillator (DCO) starts in a few microseconds and can be switched off again, so it costs almost no energy while the CPU sleeps.

problem: "one instruction adds two bytes" is unclear; a student may read it as a 16-bit add handling two memory bytes at once.
fix: a 16-bit add handles two bytes of data in one instruction, and a 16-bit pointer fits in one register.

problem: The answer 8 bits of opcode is only the arithmetic of this made-up question. The real MSP430 dual-operand format has a 4-bit opcode, two 4-bit register fields, and 4 remaining bits for the Ad, B/W and As addressing-mode fields, so a student may carry away the false idea that the MSP430 has an 8-bit opcode.
fix: Keep the arithmetic (4 + 4 = 8 bits for two register numbers, 8 bits left), and add: in the real encoding those 8 bits are not all opcode — 4 are the opcode and 4 hold the addressing-mode and byte/word bits.
